methods.label: Use equal consecutive differences
methods.explanation:
In an arithmetic progression, the two consecutive differences are equal. Rearranging that equality shows that twice the middle term equals the sum of the outer terms. Therefore,
\[2\binom n2=\binom n1+\binom n3.\]
Using the supplied factorial definition and canceling common factorial factors gives
\[n(n-1)=n+\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}6.\]
All factorial arguments are positive integers because \(n>3\). Also, \(n>0\), so we may divide by \(n\). Multiplying by six then gives
\[6(n-1)=6+(n-1)(n-2).\]
Expanding and collecting terms produces
\[0=n^2-9n+14=(n-7)(n-2).\]
A product is zero only if at least one factor is zero, so \(n=7\) or \(n=2\). The restriction \(n>3\) excludes \(2\).

For \(n=7\), the three terms are \(7,21,35\), whose consecutive differences are both \(14\). Hence \(n=7\), choice B.
